strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored setting: joint video super-resolution and deblurring when blur severity varies over time. The decomposition into degradation estimation and restoration is sensible, and conditioning both stages on exposure-related features is technically coherent.

FMA-Net++ combines several useful ideas—bidirectional hierarchical propagation, exposure-conditioned modulation, multi-hypothesis flow, and degradation-aware attention—into a clear end-to-end system. The manuscript and supplementary material provide equations, architectural details, losses, and training hyperparameters.

The reported synthetic-benchmark results are strong and consistent: FMA-Net++ improves PSNR, SSIM, and tOF over retrained baselines on REDS4-ME, REDS-RE, and GoPro, while reporting favorable parameter count and runtime. Qualitative comparisons also generally show sharper structures.

Ablations cover temporal architectures, ETE, the number of HRBP blocks and flow hypotheses, attention, filtering, and loss terms. The authors also acknowledge limitations of synthetic degradation and 2D flow modeling.
weaknesses: The central real-world dynamic-exposure claim is not adequately validated. REDS-ME/RE use normalized frame averaging followed by bicubic downsampling, so changing the nominal exposure primarily changes blur duration; it does not model exposure-dependent brightness, shot/read noise, saturation, response nonlinearity, rolling shutter, or auto-exposure/gain coupling. Thus the benchmarks are controlled synthetic blur-severity tests rather than convincing simulations of real camera exposure changes.

Real-world evidence is limited to selected smartphone examples without ground truth, capture metadata, sequence/sample counts, or a reproducible evaluation protocol. NIQE and MUSIQ on selected outputs cannot establish accurate restoration or temporal consistency and may reward hallucinated sharpness. Consequently, claims of strong real-world generalization and adaptation to continuous auto-exposure transitions are substantially stronger than the evidence supports.

The exposure component is insufficiently isolated. ETE is supervised using five synthetic exposure labels that are strongly confounded with blur extent, and no exposure-estimation accuracy or comparison against simpler blur-severity conditioning is provided. Its gain is only 0.11–0.12 dB on REDS4-ME, while deliberately incorrect guidance changes PSNR by at most 0.17 dB and can slightly outperform the no-ETE model, weakening claims that exposure conditioning is crucial or physically grounded.

The claimed long-range temporal advantage is overstated or insufficiently characterized. Each HRBP stage exchanges information only between adjacent frames, so four blocks appear to provide a limited, linearly growing receptive field rather than demonstrated full-sequence long-range modeling. There is no scaling analysis over sequence length, memory, or latency, and the construction and fairness of the sliding-window and recurrent variants are not specified sufficiently.

The method is substantially derived from FMA-Net: FGDF, degradation/restoration decomposition, flow-mask hypotheses, and multi-attention are inherited, while the principal additions are ETE/ETM and a revised propagation backbone. These additions are useful, but novelty is moderate, and the paper does not cleanly separate gains from the new backbone, exposure conditioning, and increased capacity in a matched factorial comparison.

Evaluation is restricted to ×4 restoration and largely to four REDS test clips or datasets generated with closely related frame-averaging protocols. There are no uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, tests under realistic noise/illumination shifts, or evaluation on a captured paired dataset. Baseline retraining details and runtime conditions—hardware, precision, batch/sequence length, and inclusion of all preprocessing—are also insufficient for independently verifying fairness and reproducibility.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant but underexplored setting—joint video super-resolution and deblurring under varying exposure—and is clearly written with a coherent degradation/restoration formulation.

FMA-Net++ reports strong quantitative results. On REDS4-ME it improves over retrained FMA-Net by 0.62–0.73 dB, and it also obtains substantial gains on REDS-RE and GoPro while using a moderate 12.8M parameters.
The evaluation covers numerous contemporary baselines, restoration quality, temporal consistency, runtime, synthetic cross-dataset generalization, and qualitative real-video examples.

The supplementary material provides useful implementation details, loss definitions, dataset-generation procedures, limitations, and several ablations concerning temporal modeling, ETE, multi-flow hypotheses, filtering, and losses.

The hierarchical architecture offers an attractive accuracy/efficiency trade-off: it is substantially faster than several transformer baselines and modestly outperforms the recurrent variant in the authors' controlled comparison.
weaknesses: The central claim of handling real-world dynamic exposure is not convincingly validated. REDS-ME and REDS-RE are entirely synthetic, created by averaging interpolated frames and bicubic downsampling. This omits exposure-dependent brightness, gain, shot/read noise, saturation, nonlinear ISP behavior, and spatially varying illumination. REDS-RE merely switches among these synthetic averaging levels, so it is a limited proxy for real auto-exposure.

The real-world evaluation has no ground truth, exposure metadata, or controlled capture protocol. NIQE and MUSIQ plus selected crops cannot establish that the videos contain the claimed exposure trajectories or that improvements arise specifically from exposure awareness. Statements about successful adaptation to continuous, intermediate exposure states are therefore unsupported.

Exposure time is fundamentally confounded with motion magnitude in a single blurred RGB frame. The ETE is trained using synthetic exposure-class labels, but the paper reports neither exposure-estimation accuracy nor tests that disentangle exposure duration from scene motion. Its embedding may simply encode blur severity or content rather than physical exposure.

The ETE ablation is not parameter matched: adding ETE increases the model from 9.8M to 12.8M parameters. There is no comparison to a generic or randomly supervised encoder of similar capacity. Moreover, deliberately changing guidance from 5:5 to 5:1 changes PSNR by only 0.17 dB, making the claimed central role of explicit exposure conditioning less compelling than the overall benchmark gains suggest.

The claimed 'physically grounded' degradation kernel is only indirectly conditioned on a learned image embedding and supervised reconstruction loss. No kernel ground truth, physical parameter recovery, or comparison against alternative exposure-aware degradation models is provided, so this description overstates the demonstrated evidence.

Much of the method extends FMA-Net: FGDF, multi-flow masks, degradation/restoration decoupling, and multi-attention are inherited or closely adapted. The principal additions are hierarchical propagation and SFT-style exposure modulation. These are potentially useful, but the conceptual novelty is moderate and the paper does not cleanly isolate their contributions with a full component-by-component, parameter-matched ablation.

The claim of long-range sequence-level modeling needs qualification. Each HRBP stage propagates information only between adjacent frames, and the final model uses four blocks; the effective temporal reach and scaling behavior on genuinely long sequences are not analyzed. Runtime alone also does not demonstrate the claimed parallel-training advantage through throughput or memory measurements across sequence lengths.

Benchmark reproducibility remains incomplete: the exact train/test exclusion procedure for REDS4, interpolation artifacts introduced by EMA-VFI, exposure trajectories, and whether generated data/code will be released are not clearly established. No uncertainty across runs or statistical significance is reported.

Assessed under the default Algorithms/General category, the strong empirical performance makes the decision close, but the evidence does not adequately support the paper's defining real-world, dynamic-exposure, and physically grounded claims. The balance therefore slightly favors rejection.

strengths: Evaluated as an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper addresses a meaningful and relatively underexplored setting: joint video super-resolution and deblurring under frame-varying exposure. The combination of exposure-conditioned restoration and parallel temporal propagation is well motivated for ordinary RGB cameras.

FMA-Net++ combines several coherent technical elements: HRBP blocks for bidirectional sequence-level propagation, Exposure Time-aware Modulation, exposure-aware flow-guided dynamic filtering, and a degradation/restoration decomposition. The three-stage training procedure and degradation-reconstruction supervision are technically sensible.

The empirical results are strong and consistent. On REDS4-ME, the method improves over retrained FMA-Net by 0.62–0.73 dB while reducing per-frame runtime from 0.318 s to 0.074 s. It also leads all reported methods on REDS-RE and improves substantially on GoPro, including a 1.66 dB gain over FMA-Net.

The evaluation covers restoration accuracy, structural similarity, temporal consistency, runtime, parameter count, synthetic-to-unseen-dataset generalization, and qualitative real-video behavior. Relevant SR, deblurring, blind-VSR, and joint-restoration baselines are included and mostly retrained for the proposed setting.

Ablations address the temporal architecture, ETE, number of HRBP blocks and motion hypotheses, degradation-aware attention, filtering strategy, upsampling design, and loss terms. The larger ETE improvement on REDS-RE and GoPro is encouraging evidence that exposure conditioning helps beyond the fixed-exposure training cases.

The manuscript is clear and professionally presented. The supplement provides useful implementation details, loss definitions, dataset construction procedures, sensitivity analyses, and candid limitations concerning synthetic capture and flow-based motion modeling.
weaknesses: The evidence does not fully isolate exposure awareness from additional capacity or generic blur-severity features. Removing ETE also removes roughly 3M parameters, but there is no capacity-matched feature-conditioning baseline, randomly initialized/frozen encoder, or oracle-exposure comparison. Consequently, the ETE ablation alone cannot establish that the gains specifically arise from learning exposure rather than a richer image representation.

The claim of physically grounded degradation modeling is somewhat overstated. Exposure and motion are not separately identifiable from a blurred RGB frame in general, no exposure-estimation accuracy or calibration is reported, and the learned 20×20 kernels do not appear to have explicit physical constraints such as positivity or normalization. Reconstruction supervision can admit many nonphysical kernels.

REDS-RE is constructed by mixing frames from five already synthesized discrete exposure levels, all represented during training. It therefore tests a new temporal arrangement more directly than genuinely unseen exposure values or a real auto-exposure camera process. Its four REDS4 clips are also small, and the manuscript should state the train/test exclusion and release protocol more explicitly to rule out overlap concerns.

The real-world claim relies on selected smartphone examples and no-reference image metrics, without paired ground truth, a user study, a real captured benchmark, or a temporal metric on those videos. Synthetic averaging additionally omits sensor noise, nonlinear response, saturation, rolling shutter, and the signal-to-noise changes that motivate exposure control. Thus, real-camera robustness remains promising rather than conclusively demonstrated.

With four nearest-neighbor propagation blocks, the temporal receptive field is expanded but remains bounded; it is not equivalent to the potentially unbounded context of a recurrent model. Sequence-length scaling, GPU memory, latency/throughput under a stated batching protocol, and behavior beyond the 10-frame training length are not analyzed, weakening the broad long-range and efficiency claims.

Baseline retraining and adaptation details are insufficient for complete reproducibility and fairness assessment. The paper should document input lengths, schedules, tuning budgets, event simulation for Ev-DeblurVSR, runtime hardware and measurement protocol, and whether every baseline receives equivalent access to sequence context. Code and benchmark release commitments are also not stated clearly.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored setting: joint video super-resolution and deblurring when exposure duration changes across frames. The motion/exposure coupling is well motivated, and the limitations of fixed-exposure restoration are clearly articulated.

FMA-Net++ combines a parallel temporal backbone with exposure-conditioned degradation estimation in a coherent design. Separating degradation learning from restoration and supervising the predicted degradation through input reconstruction are technically sensible choices.

The empirical results are strong. On REDS4-ME, FMA-Net++ improves over the retrained FMA-Net by 0.62–0.73 dB, and it also leads on REDS-RE and GoPro while using only 12.8M parameters and reporting substantially lower runtime than several video-transformer baselines.

The evaluation is unusually thorough in several respects: it includes accuracy, temporal consistency, runtime, memory, capacity-matched controls, alternative exposure-conditioning designs, corrupted-guidance tests, temporal-backbone variants, and component/loss ablations. The guidance-intervention experiments provide useful evidence that the exposure embedding is actively used.

REDS-ME and REDS-RE provide controlled test beds for exposure-duration variation. The synthesis process, exposure duty cycles, and random-walk trajectories are described sufficiently clearly to make the benchmark concept reproducible.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually well organized, and it appropriately acknowledges that its synthetic degradation excludes gain, noise, clipping, white balance, and other camera effects.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. The algorithmic novelty is moderate rather than fundamental: the two-network formulation, FGDF, multi-flow alignment, and degradation-aware restoration substantially inherit from FMA-Net, while ETM is an SFT-style modulation layer and HRBA is stacked bidirectional neighbor aggregation. The paper should distinguish inherited and new components more sharply.

The claim of long-range or sequence-level temporal modeling is overstated. With four HRBA blocks that exchange information only between adjacent frames, the effective temporal receptive field remains bounded by network depth rather than spanning an arbitrary full sequence. Training also uses only ten-frame clips. Experiments varying test-sequence length or reporting performance as temporal distance increases are needed to substantiate long-range generalization.

Exposure duration is not identifiable from blur alone because observed blur jointly depends on motion, exposure, depth, and scene texture. The ETE classification and t-SNE results show separation on the authors' synthetic distribution, but do not establish that ETE estimates exposure rather than dataset-specific blur severity. Guidance corruption proves reliance on the embedding, not its physical validity. Controlled cross-combinations of motion magnitude and exposure, or evaluation with measured camera exposure metadata, would provide stronger evidence.

The central dynamic-exposure evidence is largely synthetic and narrow. REDS-RE splices five discretely synthesized exposure levels with changes every five or seven frames, whereas real auto-exposure is continuous and co-varies with gain, noise, clipping, and illumination. Real-world support consists of selected examples and no-reference metrics, which are weak evidence for faithful restoration and temporal consistency without ground truth or a user study.

Some comparison and efficiency details are insufficient for firm fairness or reproducibility judgments. The manuscript does not fully specify baseline training protocols, sequence lengths used for timing, hardware and timing procedure, or how the event input required by Ev-DeblurVSR was produced. Runtime per frame can be misleading for methods with different temporal batching and memory behavior; FLOPs, peak memory for all major baselines, and standardized timing would help.

The reported gains attributable specifically to exposure conditioning are modest on the controlled fixed-exposure sets: relative to the capacity-matched no-ETE model, the full method is slightly worse at 5:4 and only 0.04 dB better at 5:5. Larger gains on REDS-RE and GoPro are encouraging, but results across random REDS-RE trajectory seeds and multiple training seeds are absent, so uncertainty around these differences is unknown.

Dataset scale, exact sample counts, benchmark/code release plans, and several implementation details needed to independently reproduce all baseline adaptations are not stated. Since the strongest claims rely on newly constructed benchmarks, public data-generation code and fixed evaluation trajectories are important.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant but underexplored setting: joint video super-resolution and deblurring with frame-varying exposure duration. In the absence of a declared contribution type, I assess it as Algorithms/General.

The architecture is coherent: HRBA provides parallel bidirectional temporal aggregation, while ETE/ETM conditions degradation estimation and restoration on inferred exposure information. Decoupling degradation learning from restoration is technically sensible.

The empirical results are consistently strong. FMA-Net++ improves over the retrained FMA-Net by 0.62–0.84 dB across REDS4-ME and REDS-RE, performs particularly well on GoPro, and reports favorable runtime and memory usage.

The ablation suite is unusually thorough. It includes capacity-matched no-ETE controls, alternative exposure-conditioning objectives, corrupted-guidance tests, fixed-input sensitivity, temporal-backbone variants, component ablations, and analyses of flow hypotheses and training losses.

REDS-ME and REDS-RE provide useful controlled test beds, and the synthesis procedure, exposure trajectories, hyperparameters, and acknowledged camera-model limitations are described in the supplement.
weaknesses: The main evidence remains dominated by synthetic data generated from REDS using 16× temporal interpolation followed by averaging. Possible EMA-VFI artifacts and the narrow blur/downsampling model may favor methods trained on the same pipeline. There is no quantitative evaluation on real videos with measured frame-wise exposure or ground-truth sharp high-resolution frames.

Exposure duration is not identifiable from blur appearance alone without accounting for motion. The ETE could therefore be learning synthetic blur magnitude or dataset-specific cues rather than exposure itself. The t-SNE and 92% k-NN results do not resolve this confound, and the cross-validation protocol is insufficiently specified, particularly regarding separation by scene/video.

The claimed real-world generalization is supported by a small set of selected qualitative examples and NIQE/MUSIQ. These no-reference metrics are not reliable substitutes for a real dynamic-exposure benchmark, and the paper does not report the amount of real-world data, exposure metadata, or a systematic human evaluation.

The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to FMA-Net: FGDF, multi-flow alignment, degradation learning, and much of the restoration design are inherited, while ETM is a standard affine feature modulation driven by a pretrained ResNet embedding. The capacity-matched ablation shows almost no gain on fixed-exposure REDS4-ME-5:5 and only a moderate 0.25 dB gain on REDS-RE, narrowing the demonstrated benefit of explicit exposure modeling.

The description overstates HRBA as long-range sequence-level modeling. With four neighbor-aggregation blocks, its receptive field is still finite and relatively local; no scaling study over sequence length or temporal distance is provided. The advantage over the recurrent variant is only 0.13 dB, and the proposed explanation involving vanishing gradients and more stable training is unsupported by gradient or training-dynamics measurements.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness are incomplete: baseline retraining schedules are not documented, runtime hardware and measurement conditions are omitted, results lack variance across training runs, and no code or benchmark release commitment is stated. These omissions weaken the otherwise strong numerical comparison.

Overall, the controlled results make a credible case for a useful contribution, but the synthetic-to-real gap, exposure/motion confounding, and incremental nature of the method prevent a confident accept. The balance slightly favors acceptance, hence a borderline score.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant and underexplored setting: joint video super-resolution and deblurring when exposure duration changes across frames. Treating motion and exposure jointly is well motivated and represents a meaningful extension beyond the fixed-exposure assumptions of FMA-Net and related restoration methods.

FMA-Net++ combines a parallelizable temporal backbone (HRBA), exposure-conditioned modulation, and degradation-aware dynamic filtering in a coherent design. Decoupling degradation estimation from restoration is technically sensible, and the method is described with sufficient mathematical and architectural detail.

The empirical results are strong. On REDS4-ME, FMA-Net++ improves over the retrained FMA-Net by 0.62–0.73 dB, while on REDS-RE and GoPro it leads the strongest reported baselines by 0.80 and 1.66 dB, respectively. It also offers an attractive accuracy/runtime/parameter trade-off, including a reported 5.2x speed advantage over RVRT at similar model size.

The ablation suite is unusually thorough. It includes capacity-matched removal of ETE, alternative exposure-conditioning objectives, corrupted-guidance tests, fixed-input sensitivity, temporal-modeling variants, component ablations, flow-hypothesis counts, degradation-filtering variants, and loss analyses. These experiments provide credible evidence that exposure guidance is actively used rather than merely adding capacity.

REDS-ME and REDS-RE provide controlled testbeds for studying exposure-dependent blur. The synthesis procedure, exposure levels, random-walk trajectories, and main training hyperparameters are documented in the supplement, supporting reproducibility. The limitations section also appropriately identifies important camera effects excluded from the benchmarks.

The presentation is clear and polished, with informative diagrams and qualitative comparisons. The paper consistently distinguishes RGB-only inference from event-dependent alternatives and reports temporal consistency in addition to per-frame fidelity.
weaknesses: The central “long-range” claim is not fully established. Each HRBA block aggregates neighboring frames, and the final model uses four blocks, apparently yielding a finite receptive field rather than unrestricted sequence-level interaction. Experiments do not report receptive-field size, accuracy versus sequence length, memory/runtime scaling with sequence length, or comparisons on genuinely long sequences. Thus, sequence-level parallel execution is demonstrated more clearly than long-range temporal modeling.

REDS-RE is derived by mixing five synthetic exposure versions of only the standard four REDS test scenes, using one structured random trajectory per scene as far as described. Results could therefore be sensitive to a very small scene set or particular random trajectories. Multiple trajectory seeds, confidence intervals, and evaluation on a larger independently captured dynamic-exposure dataset would substantially strengthen the benchmark claims.

The exposure representation may encode observed blur severity rather than exposure duration itself, since blur is jointly determined by exposure and motion. The 92% exposure-label separability and guidance-corruption experiments show that the embedding is useful, but do not establish disentanglement from motion or recovery of physical exposure. Claims about explicitly estimating exposure-dependent properties should consequently be interpreted as learned conditioning on synthetic exposure labels.

The real-world evidence is qualitative and relies on NIQE/MUSIQ, which are imperfect proxies for faithful restoration and can favor sharpening or hallucination. No-reference scores on a small displayed selection cannot by themselves validate broad real-world generalization. The GoPro preprocessing and exact x4 evaluation construction are also insufficiently specified in the manuscript.

Several efficiency and fairness details are missing: inference hardware, precision, timing protocol, baseline retraining schedules, and peak memory for most competing methods are not reported. The internally constructed recurrent and sliding-window variants also lack parameter/memory accounting, while the explanation that recurrent propagation suffers from vanishing gradients is speculative without training-dynamics evidence.

The method remains substantially based on FMA-Net components, including flow-guided dynamic filtering and degradation/restoration decomposition. The main innovations are valuable but evolutionary. Moreover, the exposure-aware gain over a capacity-matched model on REDS-RE is modest (0.25 dB), although the larger GoPro gain and extensive sensitivity analyses make the overall case sufficiently persuasive.
